title: Rounding Numbers Grade 4: Nearest 10, 100 & 1000 (+ Free Quiz)
meta_desc: Teach rounding numbers grade 4 the easy way: round to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000, estimate answers, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable worksheet.
excerpt: A shopkeeper says a phone costs about ₹15,000, not ₹14,987. That rounding instinct is exactly what Grade 4 needs. Here is how to teach rounding to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 — with a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Walk into any shop in a Tier-2 city and listen to the numbers people actually say. A phone that costs ₹14,987 becomes ‘about fifteen thousand’. A trip of 312 km becomes ‘roughly 300’. Nobody is being lazy — they are rounding, because rounded numbers are easier to hold in your head and quick to check. That everyday instinct is exactly what rounding numbers grade 4 is really about: not a classroom trick, but a way to make big numbers manageable and to catch mistakes before they matter.

By Grade 4 children are working with numbers up to lakhs, and that is where estimation earns its keep. In this post I will walk through rounding to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000, the one rule that ties it all together, and how rounding doubles as a mental check on answers. I will also touch on comparing and ordering large numbers, because the two skills lean on each other.

The one rule behind all rounding

Here is the whole thing in a sentence: look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up. If it is 4 or less, round down (keep the digit the same). Then replace everything to the right with zeros. That is it — the same rule works for tens, hundreds and thousands.

Say you are rounding 3,847 to the nearest hundred. The hundreds digit is 8. The digit to its right is 4, which is less than 5, so the 8 stays and you get 3,800. Round the same number to the nearest thousand instead: the thousands digit is 3, the digit to its right is 8 (5 or more), so it rounds up to 4,000.

Why the number line makes it click

The rule feels arbitrary until a child sees it on a number line. Draw 40 and 50 with 45 marked in the middle. Now plot a number like 43 — it sits closer to 40, so it rounds down. Plot 48 — closer to 50, rounds up. The midpoint, 45, is the tie, and by convention we round it up to 50. In my experience teaching nine-year-olds, five minutes with a hand-drawn number line does more than a page of rules. Children stop asking ‘up or down?’ once they can see which end is nearer.

Rounding to 10, 100 and 1000

The place you round to decides which digit you inspect. Watch how the same number, 6,473, changes:

Round 6,473 to the nearest…Digit to check5 or more?Answer
103 (ones)No6,470
1007 (tens)Yes6,500
10004 (hundreds)No6,000

Notice the same number rounds to three different values depending on the target place. That is the single most common Grade 4 slip — a child rounds 6,473 to 6,500 when the question asked for the nearest ten. Always read which place the question wants before touching a digit.

Rounding to estimate and check answers

This is the part I care about most, and the part most worksheets skip. Rounding is not just an exercise you finish and forget — it is a way to sanity-check a calculation. Suppose a child adds 487 + 316 and writes 703. Round first: 487 is about 500, 316 is about 300, so the answer should be near 800. 703 is close enough — the answer is reasonable. But if the child had written 173, the estimate of 800 screams that something went wrong.

  • Estimate before you calculate: round each number, add or subtract the rounded values, and you have a target to aim for.
  • Estimate after you calculate: if your exact answer is nowhere near the estimate, re-check — you have probably slipped a digit or misplaced a carry.
  • Estimate when the exact answer does not matter: ‘roughly how much for 4 notebooks at ₹38 each?’ — round 38 to 40, times 4, about ₹160.

One honest caveat: rounded estimates drift when you round several numbers the same direction. Round 48 and 47 both up and 48 + 47 (=95) becomes 50 + 50 = 100, which is a fair bit high. Teach children that an estimate is a ballpark, not the answer — useful for checking, not for the final tick.

Comparing and ordering big numbers

Rounding and comparing are cousins. To compare 45,678 and 45,321 you scan from the left, digit by digit, until they differ — the ten-thousands and thousands match, but 6 hundreds beats 3 hundreds, so 45,678 is larger. Ordering a list works the same way: line the numbers up by their place values and compare left to right. Rounding helps here too, as a first pass: if one number rounds to 46,000 and another to 45,000, you already know which is bigger without checking every digit.

A simple weekly routine

Ten focused minutes beats a marathon session. A pattern that works: two days rounding to the nearest 10 and 100, one day on the nearest 1000, one day using rounding to estimate real sums (grocery bills are perfect), and a mixed day where the child has to decide which place to round to. That deciding step — not the mechanical rounding — is where genuine number sense shows up.

Test what your child has learned

The short quiz below covers exactly this: rounding to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000, estimating to check an answer, and comparing large numbers. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions on comparing, ordering and rounding, each with a full answer key.

questions.q: About how much is 487 + 316, using rounding to the nearest 100?
questions.explanation: 487 rounds to 500 and 316 rounds to 300. 500 + 300 = 800, a good estimate of the exact 803.
Compare left to right. The first three digits match; then 7 hundreds in 45,700 beats 6, 3 and 0 hundreds in the others.
The thousands digit is 2; the digit to its right is 4 (less than 5), so it stays. Answer 12,000, even though 499 feels close to 500.

questions.q: Rounded to the nearest 10, which number does NOT become 80?
questions.explanation: 76 rounds to 80, 84 rounds to 80 and 79 rounds to 80. But 85 has a ones digit of 5, so it rounds up to 90, not 80.

faq.q: What does rounding numbers mean in Grade 4?
faq.a: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby ‘round’ number that is easier to work with — the nearest 10, 100 or 1000. In Grade 4 children round numbers up to lakhs and use rounding to estimate and check answers.

faq.q: What is the rule for rounding up or down?
faq.a: Look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, keep the digit the same. Then replace everything to the right with zeros.

faq.q: How is rounding useful for checking maths?
faq.a: Round the numbers first to get a rough target. If your exact answer is far from that estimate, you have likely made a slip — for example, 487 + 316 should land near 800, so an answer of 173 is clearly wrong.

faq.q: What is the most common rounding mistake at this age?
faq.a: Rounding to the wrong place — for instance rounding 6,473 to 6,500 when the question asked for the nearest ten (6,470). Always read which place the question wants before touching a digit.
